extracted.intended_audience: British youth and general Spectator readers seeking guidance on social conduct, argumentation, persuasion, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive rules and examples for how to conduct oneself in disputes and persuasion: when to avoid argument, how to argue (tone, method, aims), how to behave when victorious, and related social cautions (including advice for women and remarks on political arithmetic and devotion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disputes as much as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid Disputes as much as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To appear easy and well-bred, prefer improving another's notion rather than contradicting it; it requires more wit and good humour to improve than to contradict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give reasons with coolness and modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are at any time obliged to enter on an Argument, give your Reasons with the utmost Coolness and Modesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coolness and modesty scarce ever fail of making an impression on hearers; present reasons calmly to win respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dogmatism and self-importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be Dogmatical, nor show by your actions or words that you are full of yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being non-dogmatical and not vain makes others more heartily rejoice at your victory; humility increases acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retreat gracefully when cornered
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are pinched in your Argument, make your Retreat with a very good Grace: You were never positive, and are now glad to be better informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit newfound information rather than stubbornly defending a position; graceful retreat preserves reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor the Socratic method
rubrics_metrics.description: Approve the Socratical Way of Reasoning: scarce affirm anything, desire information, and thus avoid being caught in an absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By asking questions and appearing to seek information you reduce risk of error and make persuasion less confrontational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be angry because others differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more unjust or ridiculous than to be angry with another because he is not of your Opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize differences arise from varied interests, education, and means; anger at disagreement is unwarranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider others' biases and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself fairly what might have been your Opinion had you all the Biasses of Education and Interest your Adversary may possibly have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking the adversary's perspective tempers judgement and aids temperance in dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passion; it hands advantage to opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: If you contend for the Honour of Victory alone, you cannot make a more false Step than by falling into a Passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion undermines your position, causes you to forget key reasons, and gives opponents advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't scorn those who do not apprehend your reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absurd to be angry with a Man because he does not apprehend the Force of your Reasons, or gives weak ones of his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you argue for reputation, pity rather than anger the one who fails to comprehend; thank nature for your clear understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger among equals is self-damaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Among your Equals no one values your Anger, which only preys upon its Master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger punishes only its owner and is neither prudent nor conducive to ease; do not punish yourself when meeting a fool or knave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the true end of argument be information
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose to yourself the true End of Argument, which is Information; if you search purely after Truth, 'twill be almost indifferent to you where you find it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize truth-seeking over winning; valuing information reduces partisan heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the role of impartial moderator
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing procures a Man more Esteem and less Envy than if he chooses the Part of Moderator, without engaging directly on either Side in a Dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting as moderator affords impartiality, opportunities to sift matters, show judgment, and make compliments to both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: When victorious, do not rub it in
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have gained a Victory, do not push it too far; 'tis sufficient to let the Company and your Adversary see 'tis in your Power, but that you are too generous to make use of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show restraint after winning; avoid exacerbating resentment by excessive triumphalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women should avoid temptations and opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Females not of the 'Salamander' kind should avoid what Religion calls 'Temptations', and the World 'Opportunities'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarities that begin with flattering freedoms often lead gradually to ruin and infamy; shun early approaches that can lead into guilt and misery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of familiarities with male companions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid too great Familiarities with a Male Companion; such freedoms may gradually betray women from innocence to ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (story of Castilian) illustrate danger: intimacy, flattery, and delegated trust can lead to betrayal and catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust men who profess love with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust not a Man; when a Man talks of Love, with Caution trust him: But if he Swears, he'll certainly deceive thee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat protestations of love skeptically; do not rely solely on words of passion when prudence is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical strategy: persuade by appealing to self-interest and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: When persuading a man to marry rather than keep a mistress, argue from both the man's interest (steadier pleasure, gratitude, social ease) and the woman's virtue (obedience, tenderness, sincere friendship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete contrasts: fleeting debauchery leads to satiety and shame; marriage promises lasting companionship, gratitude, and social respectability. Appeal to his advantage as well as moral considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political-arithmetic principle: people create wealth and revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prince's riches increase or decrease in proportion to the Number and Riches of his Subjects; assess a subject's value by what he pays (consumption, customs, excises, house-rent, land-tax).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use per-capita calculations (e.g., poor subjects contribute shillings yearly via taxes) to argue policy about population and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing land without people can reduce national value
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding equal extent of land and produce but no people would not necessarily increase the nation's riches or revenue; overproduction can depress prices and lower tax yield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doubling production beyond demand reduces prices sharply; an extended country without corresponding population may pay far less tax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abundance can reduce incentive and living standards
rubrics_metrics.description: In Countries of the greatest Plenty there is the poorest Living; when basic subsistence is easily obtained, labour incentive diminishes and consumption patterns change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If labour is only needed intermittently to secure subsistence, workers will not labour the rest of the time; this affects wages, prices, and tax revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Season a child's passions with devotion early
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of the last Importance to season the Passions of a Child with Devotion, which seldom dies in a Mind that has received an early Tincture of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early religious instruction tends to persist and later re-emerge with age, discretion, or misfortune; devotion opens the mind to sublime ideas and warms the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate devotion with reason to avoid enthusiasm and superstition
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotion, when not moderated by right Reason, is apt to degenerate into Enthusiasm; Superstition is the excess of Religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard reason as cool guide; beware of imaginary raptures and of ceremonies that ossify into childish superstitions (example: ceremonial accretions in the Roman Church).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between healthy piety and its excesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong, steady masculine Piety is glorious, but Enthusiasm is like madness and Superstition like folly; both expose reason to scorn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate steady devotion without allowing it to produce fanaticism or ritualized superstition that undermines reason.
